items.body: Three Idaho charter schools provide vastly different paths to getting students down the graduation line. Students at Valor Classical Academy follow a set of six virtues, including self-government and perseverance. A student wants to be a mom when she grows up. Students at Idaho Arts Charter School can take dance, choir, piano, ceramics and theatre. General education classes often have an art aspect. One student wants to be a silversmith, another wants to teach guitar. Students at Elevate Academy Nampa take classes in eight trades, including construction, medical arts and culinary. One student wants to graduate as a certified nursing assistant and join the military. The Idaho Charter School Association last week hosted tours of public charter schools in Caldwell, Middleton, Nampa and Kuna for legislators and journalists. “They’re making big decisions for our schools and we want to make sure that they have all the knowledge and information they need about charters to make really informed decisions,” Executive Director Nanette Merrill said. The organization invited all legislators and candidates from districts 10 and 22, but only Sen. Tammy Nichols, R-Middleton, and candidates Nancy Parker and Loren Petty showed up. On Thursday, attendees visited Valor Classical Academy in Kuna, Idaho Arts Charter School in Nampa and Elevate Academy Nampa. Each tour included pre-planned classroom visits followed by a panel discussion with selected parents and students. items.body: Every two years, something unusual happens in Idaho: every single member of the Legislature is up for election. All 70 members of the Idaho House face the voters. So do all 35 members of the Idaho Senate. That means every legislator in Boise operates on essentially the same political clock. Every two years, every seat is on the ballot, every incumbent is potentially campaigning, and every member knows the next primary is never far away. We should change that. Idaho should keep two-year terms for members of the House but move state senators to four-year terms, staggered so roughly half the Senate is elected every two years. It would make the Senate more deliberative, provide greater continuity in state government, reduce some of the election-year incentives for political theater and strengthen the Legislature’s ability to serve as a check on the permanent bureaucracy. Most importantly, it would create a meaningful institutional difference between Idaho’s two legislative chambers. After all, if we’re going to have a House and a Senate, they shouldn’t simply be two versions of the same thing. The Idaho Constitution currently gives representatives and senators the same two-year terms. The House is larger and the Senate smaller, but members of both chambers face voters on precisely the same schedule. That’s not how most states do it. And there is a reason. The two chambers of a legislature are supposed to serve somewhat different purposes. The House should be the chamber closest to the people and most immediately responsive to shifts in public opinion. Its members should return to voters frequently. Two-year terms make sense. The Senate should be different. A Senate is traditionally the smaller and more deliberative legislative body. Its members should have greater opportunity to take a longer view, develop expertise and provide continuity as political winds change. That doesn’t make senators more important than representatives. It gives them a different institutional role. Consider the political life of a newly elected Idaho senator. Win an election in November. Go to Boise in January. Serve one legislative session. Spend the interim knowing another election is approaching. Return for a second session—and by then the primary election is only months away. Then start all over again. There is barely time to govern before it’s time to campaign. Today, every one of Idaho’s 105 legislative seats appears on the ballot at the same time. Theoretically, a single election could send 105 brand-new legislators to Boise. Some Idahoans might hear that and say: Good. There is something appealing about a clean sweep. Turnover can bring fresh ideas, disrupt comfortable relationships and remind elected officials that the offices they occupy belong to the people. But there is another side to that equation. If every legislator is new, state government isn’t. The agencies are still there. The departments are still there. The administrative rules, budget processes and government programs are still there. And the career employees who have spent years—or decades—working inside that system are still there. One of the Legislature’s most important responsibilities is overseeing the executive branch and the permanent bureaucracy beneath it. Lawmakers control appropriations, write the laws agencies implement and are supposed to ask hard questions on behalf of taxpayers. To do that effectively, legislators need expertise of their own. That’s an important point for those of us who believe in limited government. Limiting government isn’t only about asking how much power government possesses. We should also care about where that power resides and who exercises it. When institutional knowledge is concentrated in the executive agencies while legislators are perpetually inexperienced, the balance of power tilts toward the permanent government. items.summary: A Flock Automated License Plate Reader near the Lowe's on Overland Road in Boise, as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. items.body: A Flock Automated License Plate Reader near the Lowe's on Overland Road in Boise, as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun) Congressman Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho (Photo courtesy of Russ Fulcher’s official website) Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher signed on to federal legislation to limit federal law enforcement’s access to data from automated license plate readers, like Flock cameras, and other surveillance equipment. Fulcher announced Monday in a press release that he is co-sponsoring H.R. 9716 , called the Protecting Rights in Video and Equipment Acquired Discovery Act, or Privacy Act. The legislation would, in most cases, require federal law enforcement to obtain a warrant from a federal judge before accessing surveillance data from state and local systems, including cameras that capture images of vehicle occupants, long-range microphones, electronic fingerprint detection technology, and “substantially similar technology” as determined by the U.S. attorney general, according to the press release. “I’m proud to sign on to this legislation to protect the privacy rights of Idahoans from increasingly intrusive surveillance data collection and to prohibit the widespread deployment of such surveillance tools with federal dollars,” Fulcher said in the press release. “It’s simple: if the federal government wants to access state and local systems’ data on citizens, they need to get a warrant.” The legislation would also put time limits on the retention of data federal authorities obtained, unless a court authorizes an extension or the data is needed as evidence for ongoing prosecution. The bill would also prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase or install surveillance devices, with some exceptions for systems used solely for toll collections on federally funded highways, school violence prevention programs, grants provided under the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act, and portable systems for specific law enforcement operations with a warrant. The bill, brought by Texas Republican U.S. Rep. Keith Self, was introduced July 15 and has not yet been voted on by a committee. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idahoans have expressed concerns about surveillance cameras A number of Idaho cities statewide have contracts for automated license plate readers, called ALPRs, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Flock is the most common and well-known brand of this type of camera. In July, nearly 100 residents filled the Caldwell City Council chambers, and about a dozen of them spoke about their concern about the city’s use of Flock cameras , the Idaho Press reported. All eyes on Flock as Idaho navigates surveillance technology across the state A 2025 Idaho state law prevents these readers from being used for anything other than “the investigation of felony, misdemeanor crimes, traffic accidents or to search for missing or endangered persons.” However, Twin Falls cameras were searched at least 631 times in March, May and June of 2026 for immigration-related searches, the Sun reported. The searches originated from outside Idaho, and later the Twin Falls Police Department changed its network sharing policies to avoid inadvertently running afoul of Idaho law and its own restrictions on immigration searches. In March, then-Jerome County Sheriff George Oppedyk used Flock cameras to search for his wife’s vehicle hundreds of times between July and September 2025, KMVT reported. Oppedyk retired in April. In early August, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers across the nation had been charged with or accused of misusing the cameras to track women. Fulcher’s office regularly polls constituents who email him, and recent polls found that data privacy was one of their top concerns, Fulcher told the Idaho Capital Sun in an Aug. 12 interview. “The data privacy stuff, especially recently with the Flock cameras, that has got a lot of people on edge,” Fulcher said. items.body: A replica of the Liberty Bell sits outside of the Idaho Statehouse, as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In May 1950, Idaho’s very own version of the Liberty Bell arrived in the Gem State. Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) Nearly a year later, the bell found its home: Sitting prominently in front of grand steps leading up to the Idaho State Capitol — and being loudly rung by passersby. But before it was mounted at the state’s Capitol, the bell toured the state on the back of a pickup truck. And as Americans commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday this year, Idaho’s Liberty Bell is headed back on tour . “We want to have people experience the birth of a nation,” Idaho Treasurer Julie Ellsworth said in an interview. “… We want a memorable thing that touches every place of Idaho.” The tour starts Wednesday with a round of stops in East Idaho, starting in Pocatello and working its way further east, before visiting each of the state’s 44 counties. But how did Idaho even get its own version of the Liberty Bell? The bell — modeled after the cracked original in Philadelphia that has become a national symbol — was one of many cast and given to states in an effort to sell U.S. savings bonds, according to a history of the bell prepared by the Idaho State Historical Society. Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell, moved from its typical home, sits on the back of a Ford F-450 flatbed truck. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Trucking a state artifact This will be one of the few instances — outside of its recent restoration — when Idaho’s Liberty Bell has left its home at the Capitol. State officials designed this tour to mimic the original tour of the bell from 76 years ago. On its journey across Idaho, the state’s Liberty Bell will sit on the rear axle of a flatbed Ford F-450 pickup. The state is leasing the custom truck for free from Kendall Ford, an auto dealer in the Boise area, Ellsworth said. The new truck has a few more bells and whistles than the original truck had — like enhanced suspension and Spudjamin Franklin, one of many “Revolutionary Spuds” that the state treasurer created to celebrate America’s 250th anniversary. But it’s also missing something that the original truck, a custom Ford R-5 flatbed, had: a loudspeaker, which was used to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds, according to Janet Gallimore, the executive director of the Idaho State Historical Society, which cares for the state’s artifacts and helped plan the bell’s recent restoration. The 1950 tour of Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell was to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) “I … just love the symbology of the bell and what it means, what it meant for obviously the beginnings of our country and the founding of our country, but what that idea of liberty, justice, self-government means to people today. Because it’s a powerful symbol of those things that make us American,” she said in an interview. On the road, the bell will be encased in a cloth cover. At its stops in each county, it will remain on the bed of the truck for display. When will Idaho’s Liberty Bell be near you? Officials aren’t releasing a daily schedule of where the bell will be in each town at a given time until closer to the dates. But Ellsworth says every child that they see on this tour will get a copy of Spudjamin Franklin’s new graphic novel-styled autobiography, which she wrote. Ellsworth said she’ll try to join the tour as much as she can. “It is so symbolic of everything about liberty,” she said of the bell. “But it’s tangible. It’s touchable. It’s understandable.” On Wednesday, the bell will make its journey from Boise to Pocatello — before beginning a nearly three-week tour across East Idaho. (Photo by Jacob Fischler/States Newsroom) A Massachusetts federal judge on Monday declined the Trump administration’s request to overturn the temporary restraining order she signed last week that blocks the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a r
items.body: A ballot drop box in Kitsap County, Washington, pictured Aug. 29, 2026. Washington is one of the eight states that conducts elections entirely by mail. (Photo by Jacob Fischler/States Newsroom) A Massachusetts federal judge on Monday declined the Trump administration’s request to overturn the temporary restraining order she signed last week that blocks the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a rule placing new restrictions on mail-in voting. The 14-day order published Aug. 27 was not appealable, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote in a brief order Monday . But even if the order could be appealed, the administration would lose on the merits, Talwani wrote. “It is likely that the USPS lacked authority to issue the Final Rule and that the Final Rule is substantively unconstitutional and contrary to law,” she wrote. She dismissed the administration’s argument that the temporary restraining order came too close to Election Day as a “cynical interpretation” of the U.S. Supreme Court’s Aug. 24 decision that allowed President Donald Trump’s related executive order to move forward on procedural grounds. The high court found that Trump’s executive order, which directed the Postal Service to create the rule, could not be challenged until the rule itself was in place. It made no determination on the merits of the rule. “A Final Rule has now issued and, contrary to Defendants’ cynical interpretation, the Supreme Court has not endorsed the view that any challenge to the Final Rule is now too late,” Talwani, whom President Barack Obama appointed to the bench, wrote. She added that she disagreed with the USPS argument that the requirements of the rule, which would force states to overhaul their vote-by-mail systems ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections and to gain federal government approval of lists of voters who requested mail ballots, were “modest.” The administration is also fighting Democratic-led states and voting rights groups in the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals over Talwani’s temporary restraining order and in Talwani’s court over a longer pause of the final rule. Several Republican state attorneys general, representing Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas, joined the suit on the federal government’s side. The rule’s challengers say it is an inappropriate incursion of states’ power to administer elections, and would likely disenfranchise people who depend on mail ballots to vote. Trump has long claimed, without evidence, and despite his personal use of the service, that mail voting enables election fraud. The administration has said its rule is needed to ensure that noncitizens do not vote in federal elections, which studies have shown is rare. Trump issued the executive order March 31. States and voting rights groups immediately sued to stop it, but the legal battle heated up last week with the Supreme Court’s procedural decision on its emergency docket. The states and groups challenging the law quickly refiled their lawsuits to reflect that the rule had been published Aug. 21.

items.summary: Boise State University is denying wrongdoing in a public records dispute with a conservative lobbying group. Attorneys for Boise State say the university “acted in good faith” in responding to the Idaho Family Policy Center — even though the group received only two pages of university records, at a cost of $257.02. The IFPC filed a lawsuit on July 24 , stemming from a seven-month records dispute.
items.body: Boise State University is denying wrongdoing in a public records dispute with a conservative lobbying group. Attorneys for Boise State say the university “acted in good faith” in responding to the Idaho Family Policy Center — even though the group received only two pages of university records, at a cost of $257.02. The IFPC filed a lawsuit on July 24 , stemming from a seven-month records dispute. The Christian lobbying group requested documents, data and correspondence related to a 2025 article authored by two Boise State researchers. The article said 35% of OB-GYNs left Idaho between 2022 and 2024, in the wake of the state’s near-total ban on abortion. The IFPC authored one of Idaho’s anti-abortion laws. The lawsuit alleges Boise State dragged out its response to the request for more than a month, withheld germane documents and charged for a costly legal review of the records that ultimately were released. “By refusing multiple requests for these documents, and rebuffing efforts to solve this matter without litigation, BSU has frivolously pursued its refusal,” the IFPC said in its lawsuit. In a response filed Tuesday, Boise State said it produced all documents that fell within the parameters of the request and did not delay its response. The university also defended the bill that it sent to the IFPC — which reflected 6.5 hours of staff review, including 3 hours of legal work. Idaho’s public records law is based in a presumption of openness. In other words, documents are considered public records unless they are specifically exempt from disclosure. The dispute between Boise State and the IFPC centers on two intertwined issues. The timing . The law requires public entities to release records to Idaho residents within three working days — although agencies can and frequently do claim an extension that pushes the timetable to 10 working days. In this case, IFPC policy analyst Grace Howat filed a records request on Dec. 10. Boise State responded on Dec. 23, within 10 working days. The university did not produce the records at this time, but instead sent an estimate — reflecting the potential cost of reviewing and producing the records. Boise State did not request payment at this time. On Jan. 8, Boise State sent a $257.02 invoice. IFPC paid the bill that day. Howat twice sent followup emails, asking about the status of the records request. “Am I able to receive the records I requested and paid for?” she wrote on Jan. 26. The university provided the two-page response on Jan. 27 — more than 10 working days after IFPC paid the invoice. But in Boise State’s response in court, attorneys defended the turnaround time. “(Boise State) denies (IFPC’s) characterization that (Boise State) ‘sat on the request for over a month.’” Carsten Peterson and Eric Stokes are representing Boise State in the case. They work for Hawley Troxell , a Boise-based firm prominent in education law . The invoice . Public agencies are required to cover some cost of retrieving records — their first two hours of staff time and the first 100 pages of paper records. Beyond that, agencies are allowed to bill their costs, but they aren’t required to do so. Boise State says the $257.02 invoice covers 6.5 hours of staff review, above the two “free” hours of employee time. IFPC is skeptical, noting that the two pages released by Boise State were unredacted. In their response, Boise State’s attorneys say that staff had to review documents beyond the two pages that were released. “(Boise State) denies the inference that 6 1/2 hours responding to Ms. Howat’s request was excessive.” What’s next? It’s unclear when the dispute may go to court. Both sides are seeking their costs and attorney’s fees. IFPC is also seeking the $257.02 in question, or a cost to be determined at trial. items.body: Crews are completing the new Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County. (Photo by Julia Barton/Greater Yellowstone Coalition) Crews are nearing completion of a new wildlife underpass in southeast Idaho after the public, nonprofit agencies, conservation groups and government agencies pushed for years to protect migrating wildlife herds and drivers. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass is expected to be completed this fall along U.S. Highway 30, south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County, public officials and conservationists announced jointly this week. The wildlife crossing features three underpasses, as well as extensive fencing on either side of the project to direct animals like deer to the wildlife crossing. “We were seeing just all kinds of problems there; we were losing at least 100 deer a year,” Idaho Transportation Department public information officer Justin Smith said in an interview Wednesday. “Over 10 years, that is 1,000 animals we know we lost.” Officials also said those collisions cost drivers and taxpayers millions of dollars every year. “Our primary concern is the safety of the traveling public. Whether they are going through a construction zone or whether they are in a wildlife area, we want to keep people safe on our highways, and this is part of that effort,” Smith said. The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass represents a partnership between the Idaho Transportation Department, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, the Idaho Conservation League and Bear Lake County, officials said. This map depicts the project area for the Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier. (Map courtesy of Greater Yellowstone Coalition) “Rocky Point shows what’s possible when agencies, conservation and sporting groups and local communities work toward the same goal,” Matt Lucia, Idaho conservation manager at the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, said in a written statement. “(The Greater Yellowstone Coalition) has been part of this project for years — contributing time, energy and funds toward the effort. The next step is making sure the federal funding that made this project possible stays available.” To build the crossing, the Idaho Transportation Department secured a $20.8 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration’s Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program. Funding comes from the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that was passed by Congress and signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021. The federal grant was estimated to cover 98% of the construction costs, but the project may come in under budget, allowing the state to return some of the money to the Federal Highway Administration, Smith said. In 2023, crews built the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass on Idaho Highway 21 near Lucky Peak, between Boise and Idaho City. The Cervidae overpass features more than one mile of big game fencing to direct the animals to the safe crossing. Fish and Game officials installed a wildlife camera at the crossing to document how it is working. (Getty Images) An advisory group has identified Idaho counties at high risk for opioid use disorder to target in its recommendations for the state’s use of opioid settlement funds. The Idaho Behavioral Health Council brings together the state’s three branches of government — legislative, judicial and executive — to provide recommendations to lawmakers about how to improve mental health and substance use issues statewide. The council on Friday finalized its recommendation that opioid settlement funds be prioritized for at-risk populations and communities. A summary highlighting some of the counties facing the highest risk of opioid use disorder included Kootenai, Benewah, Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Clearwater, Boise and Ada counties. The state’s opioid settlement fund was created from a nationwide settlement with opioid manufacturers and may be used for certain, approved prevention or treatment projects. Last year, the Legislature approved spending $6.8 million of opioid settlement funds, according to a memo from the Division of Financial Management. Idaho Behavioral Health Council asks lawmakers to prioritize rural communities with opioid funding The council voted on its top priorities at a meeting in June, which included funding proposed for projects that focus on prevention for high-risk populations, behavioral health support for first responders, and developing the behavioral health workforce. Council members on Friday agreed to send a one-page summary outlining risk factors for opioid use disorder and highlighting which counties were most at-risk, using a 2024 report titled the Opioid-Related Overdose Vulnerability in Idaho: An Epidemiological Assessment. “This handout identifies risk factors for opioid use disorder and puts them in the context of Idaho, where those places are, where we may have more vulnerable folks, where we have had higher levels of overdose, where we have high levels of opioid prescriptions being written,” said Sara Omundson, administrative director of state courts and co-chair of the Behavioral Health Council. “All of this is based on research that was done over the last few years.” The council also agreed to ask the governor and state legislative budget writers to prioritize projects that serve rural communities in the state. Factors that may lead to certain populations to be at higher risk of misusing opioids include lower educational attainment, according to the risk factor summary the council included with its recommendations. Those without college experience are almost twice as likely to misuse opioids, the summary said. The summary also identified other Idaho counties at-risk because of factors such as high prescription rates and high narcotic arrests using data from the American Community Survey , the Idaho Prescription Drug Monitoring Program , and the Idaho State Police Statistical Analysis Center. The top counties at risk based on low average educational attainment are Shoshone, Lincoln, Minidoka, Owyhee, Adams, Benewah, Payette, Gooding, Jerome and Clark counties. The top counties for high opioid prescription rates are Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Butte, Lewis, Shoshone, Benewah, Caribou, Gem and Lemhi. items.body: Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the ballot initiative in Idaho to restore abortion access, speaks to supporters at the Idaho Capitol in July. The nonprofit she leads, Idahoans United for Women and Families, is suing the state over a final segment of ballot language that will also appear in the statewide voter pamphlet. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) BOISE, Idaho — The group leading the effort to restore abortion access by ballot initiative in Idaho has filed a lawsuit against state officials over proposed language that will appear on the ballot and in a state-issued voter pamphlet. Idahoans United for Women and Families, the nonprofit organization that drafted the initiative — now called Proposition 1 — says the “yes” and “no” statements as prepared by Idaho officials violate the law guiding the initiative process and are confusing and misleading. Attorneys filed the lawsuit to the Idaho Supreme Court late Wednesday night. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane stressed that the issue needs to be quickly resolved to meet upcoming ballot deadlines. The voter pamphlet must be printed by September 25, according to the law, and ballots need to be mailed to military and overseas voters about a week before that. McGrane said the state has paused production amid the litigation on the 850,000 copies of the voter pamphlet that need to be printed and mailed. “There was a good-faith effort to try and reflect each of the sides of the pro and con statements that were submitted to us,” McGrane told Stateline by phone on Thursday. “I think one of the biggest challenges that we’re going to see with Proposition 1 is that it’s a very complicated issue with a lot of nuance … and this isn’t a simple issue to consolidate down into a short, one-sentence statement.” Following the law, McGrane developed the language for the statements with Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, who has been outspoken in his anti-abortion views for many years and recently appealed a federal judge’s decision that would protect abortion access in cases of threats to a pregnant patient’s physical and mental health. Labrador told Stateline in an emailed statement that his duty alongside the secretary was to clearly and concisely explain the effects of a “yes” or “no” vote and to fully inform Idaho voters, and said they applied the same legal standard to every measure that has been on the ballot. “Idaho voters deserve a straightforward explanation of what their vote will do,” Labrador said. Idaho Supreme Court orders officials to revise abortion ballot initiative language, impact statement There have been similar legal fights over abortion ballot language in other states. Activists on both sides of the issue in Missouri, for example, have spent years arguing over ballot language , both on the 2024 citizen-led amendment that restored legal access to abortion, and on the 2026 amendment referred by the legislature that would reinstate the ban. Similar battles between Republican state officials and initiative organizers played out in Ohio , Arizona and Montana between 2023 and 2024. Voters in all three of those states ultimately approved amendments to protect abortion rights. It’s also not the first time Idahoans United for Women and Families has sued the state over ballot language. In April 2025, the Idaho Supreme Court heard arguments in the lawsuit, including whether the short ballot title and fiscal impact statement should be revised, and unanimously sided with Idahoans United on those two elements. Under Idaho law , the ballot must include a clear and concise statement about the effect of a “yes” or “no” vote, and the voter pamphlet must include a complete copy of the initiative text, its fiscal impact, and arguments for or against the measure with rebuttals. (Kevin Richert/Idaho EdNews) Heading to a meeting, flanked by House GOP Caucus Chair Jaron Crane, Moyle wasted no time getting to the point — Pemberton’s bill to rebrand Lewis-Clark State College as the state’s fourth full-fledged university. “He commented in passing that he hadn’t had time to ‘kill it yet,’” Pemberton, LC State’s president, said in subsequent emails to two other lawmakers. Pemberton stands by her account. When EdNews asked Moyle about the exchange this week, he chuckled. “She was persistent in the hallway all the time. I was just giving her a hard time.” Either way, the bill died, without a House hearing. Moyle, R-Star, insists he didn’t kill it, but says he doesn’t support the name change. Pemberton pledges to try again in 2027. “I better try one more time,” Pemberton said in an EdNews interview last week. “The campus community wants me to try again.” While renaming sounds cosmetic and simple, branding is essential. Supporters say university status better reflects a 133-year-old institution offering everything from associate’s degrees to master’s programs. A name is how an institution of higher learning markets itself to would-be students, prospective faculty members and possible business partners. A one-word change can change a lot. And the LC State renaming proposal was the most significant higher ed policy bill from the 2026 session. Emails between Pemberton and legislators — obtained by Idaho Education News through a public records request — offer an unusual and unfiltered behind-the-scenes look at how this bill died. The name change sailed through the Senate, but ran into high-placed resistance in the House, from Moyle and from his newly appointed House Education Committee chairman. A rebrand aligns LC State with Idaho’s four-year universities — and distinguishes LC State from the public two-year schools that have “college” in their name. University status brings LC State in line with other teaching-oriented institutions in the West. It would help LC State compete with a new wave of competition: out-of-state online schools with “university” in their title. Pemberton sees it as simple marketing. (File photo courtesy of the Idaho State Department of Agriculture) Idaho state officials say they are continuing to push for full eradication of quagga mussels after again detecting the invasive species in the Snake River near Twin Falls earlier this month. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Although quagga mussels and larvae are small, state officials and conservationists say they cause giant problems because of how rapidly they reproduce. A mussel infestation can clog pipes used for irrigation and drinking water, which could have serious effects on the state’s economy, agriculture and recreation industries, officials said. “Our outlook is that not treating this infestation is not an option,” said Sydney Kennedy, a public information officer for the Idaho State Department of Agriculture said in an interview Wednesday. Gov. Brad Little agrees. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Other states have shown us what happens when invasive mussel infestations are allowed to establish before action is taken,” Little said in a written statement. “Those delayed responses have resulted in significant long-term management costs coming directly out of taxpayer pockets. Idaho has set the standard by responding aggressively. Our responsible strategy on the Snake River is proving to be effective, and we will continue making decisions that give us the best opportunity to eliminate quagga mussels to protect Idaho’s waters and the people who depend on them.” More than 1,700 different users, including municipal drinking water systems, depend on water from the Snake River, according to the state. Officials at the nonprofit Idaho Conservation League call the detection and presence of quagga mussels a no-win situation and one of the primary threats to the health of the Snake River. This month’s detection marks four consecutive years of finding quagga mussels in the Snake River near Twin Falls. In September 2023, state officials announced for the first time they had detected invasive quagga mussel larvae in water samples . Since 2023, the portion of the river where quagga mussels have been detected has shrunk, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture said. Fewer quagga mussels detected so far this year in Snake River State officials say the number of quagga mussels detected this year is down by 77% compared to last year. As of Aug. 14, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture has detected eight quagga mussel larvae, which are known as veligers, and seven adult quagga mussels. “We know what is at stake if invasive mussels gain a foothold in Idaho,” Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt said in a written statement. “Our previous treatments have proven to be effective, and this level of containment is unprecedented among known quagga mussel infestations. items.body: U.S. District Judge B. Lynn Winmill ruled earlier this month that the state of Idaho cannot regulate abortion when a pregnancy threatens a person’s physical or mental health. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the decision, and the judge narrowed the ruling to only apply to the Boise doctor that challenged the law. (Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun) An Idaho federal judge has narrowed a previous ruling that had allowed abortions to protect a mother’s health or from self-harm to only apply to the Boise doctor who challenged the law. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) The narrowed ruling issued Tuesday means that Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and the Ada County prosecutor may not enforce Idaho’s felony abortion ban in cases where Dr. Stacy Seyb administered the procedure because of serious risk of harm due to physical health or mental health concerns. Other doctors in Idaho will still be subject to Idaho’s near-total ban, which includes an exception to prevent the death of the mother but does not include exceptions to prevent her death from self-harm. Elective abortions are completely banned in Idaho. U.S. District Court of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill narrowed the ruling at the request of Labrador, who argued in a recent motion that Winmill’s initial decision was too broad. Winmill agreed with Labrador, citing recent U.S. Supreme Court cases that ruled federal judges in most situations cannot issue “universal injunctions,” which block laws nationwide or more broadly than against the plaintiffs in the case. Winmill wrote “an injunction limited to Dr. Seyb will suffice to address the alleged harm.” Seyb was represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice in the case. “While we are disappointed in the ruling, it is only one step in the litigation,” Tanya Pellegrini, co-director of litigation at the Lawyering Project said in an emailed statement. “We will continue to stand with providers and their patients to ensure it is safe to be pregnant in Idaho.” Seyb is a maternal-fetal medicine physician who specializes in high-risk pregnancies. He challenged Idaho’s laws, testifying in court that he’s sent patients out of state amid health concerns because he did not feel comfortable providing abortions under the limited exceptions in Idaho’s law. Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows an abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license. The judge denied Labrador’s request to fully eliminate the block on enforcement. Winmill remained “persuaded” abortions to protect women against serious health risks or against death from self-harm were constitutionally protected. Labrador on Aug. 20 also appealed Winmill’s decision to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, arguing the block defies the U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. items.body: Maureen Newton waves as she uses binoculars to watch U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees board a plane on Aug. 11, 2026, at the Magic Valley Regional Airport. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around 20 men got out of the vans and boarded the plane as law enforcement oversaw the process, which took just over 30 minutes. One man was escorted back off the plane and into a van. According to a flight tracker, the plane then traveled to King County International Airport, or Boeing Field, which is located south of Seattle. Similar flights, operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, happen every Tuesday and Thursday at the Magic Valley airport. Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel record the entire boarding process for each ICE flight that operates out of the airport near Twin Falls. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel, who live about 30 minutes outside of Twin Falls, have watched every flight since they became involved in efforts to observe them on May 12. The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April. An ICE spokesperson told the Idaho Capital Sun the air operations provide “a network of air transportation to Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) 25 field offices to facilitate the movement of illegal aliens within the United States and their removal to destinations worldwide via air charter and commercial charter services.” “ICE is committed to the safety and welfare of those in custody throughout the entire transfer and removal process,” the spokesperson, who did not provide a name, said in an email. The spokesperson said in the Aug. 12 email that the agency had conducted 20 missions at the Magic Valley airport, also called Joslin Field. The agency’s Salt Lake City Field Office, which oversees Idaho, requests the flights “to support their operations which include the Magic Valley Region.” The Human Rights First ICE flight monitor has recorded 33 flights out of Twin Falls in 2026, and three flights out of the Boise airport. No other Idaho cities are listed. The federal immigration agency has a $1.8 billion contract with CSI Aviation, a private charter and cargo air transportation company, to operate the flights nationwide, according to federal spending data. Airport Manager Matt Barnes told the Sun in an email that the local airport does not have any formal agreement with ICE or CSI Aviation. “We are a public use airport that accepts federal grant funds, so we may not discriminate against aircraft operators who can safely operate at our facility,” Barnes said. ‘I think it’s wrong’; observers watch ICE flights because of due process concerns. Idaho lawmaker says operations enforce ‘rule of law’ Maureen Newton, left, and Karen Stroder, observe an ICE flight on Aug. 11, 2026, out of the Magic Valley Regional Airport. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Karen Stroder has lived in Twin Falls nearly 30 years and in Idaho her entire life, she said. She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization. “I think it’s wrong,” Stroder said of the flights. “I don’t think people are getting due process. I think everybody deserves their day in court.” Twin Falls resident Heather Muth, who helped found the local Indivisible group, learned from an Indiana chapter member that these flights were happening and that various groups tracked and recorded them. items.body: Middleton School District trustees approved a name and tabled construction bids for the new elementary school at a special Tuesday afternoon meeting. The board tabled voting on a bid package for the new elementary school’s construction because potential bidders were not able to prepare bids in time. It will meet again next week to vote. The new Freedom Elementary, a name voted on by district constituents, won’t be far — in nomenclature or distance — from Independence Elementary, a new elementary school on the West Ada School District side of Star. Middleton’s new elementary will be located on the Canyon County side of Star, a city in two counties. It will serve one of the state’s fastest-growing areas and alleviate overcrowding in two elementary schools. In other action, trustees approved language for a $3 million supplemental levy, spread over two years, to fund teaching and classified positions, new curriculum, school resource officers, classroom technology and a “hot topic:” extracurricular transportation. The deadline for districts to submit ballot language is Friday, Aug. 28. After a failed supplemental levy in May, Middleton administrators made a round of cuts to staff, curricula and logistics. Constituents have been particularly frustrated by the lack of busing for extracurricular activities like sports, trustees said. Superintendent Marc Gee also presented language for a $2.8 million levy, an increase of about $2 per year per $100,000 of property value to taxpayers, over the $3 million option. Trustees didn’t like it. “I would say two dollars makes a big difference when it comes to taking care of our schools that we’re jamming full,” Dempsey said in favor of running the larger $3 million levy. Trustee Jay Clark suggested putting the transportation issue front-and-center in the levy. “That should give us some more votes, if that’s a hot topic,” Clark said. Trustees also approved a list of potential mascots for the new school: Elementary students will vote to choose between being Eagles, Falcons, Pioneers, Patriots or Stars. The forensics lab’s construction is funded through state general funds appropriated in 2022 through House Bill 779. State law enforcement officials broke ground Tuesday on a new forensics laboratory that they hope will improve the state’s already-fast processing of criminal forensics evidence. And they hope that the $29 million forensics laboratory , based at Idaho State Police’s Headquarters in Meridian, will streamline lab services that are tapped by local and county law enforcement agencies across the state. Moments before officials ceremonially lifted dirt with shovels, Gov. Brad Little talked about the need for the facility in a state that has grown at a record pace in recent years. “The people that have been here expect a safe environment. And you can’t have effective law enforcement if you don’t have the tools that they need to do their job,” Little said. Officials expect construction on the lab to finish in January 2028. The new facility will help aid DNA testing, including advancements to establish Whole Genome Sequencing; examining latent prints; forensics for digital devices; and house technology to help solve gun-related crimes through the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network, officials say. Idaho State Police’s director, Col. Bill Gardiner, praised the agency’s forensics unit as world-renowned and says the laboratory’s construction shows the state’s investment in public safety. “It really is a reflection of those victims and them seeking justice, and those victims seeking closure,” he said before the groundbreaking ceremony. “And that’s really what this lab is there to do: provide that evidence in order to accomplish that.” Right now, Idaho State Police have an average turnaround time for DNA tests of around 30 to 45 days, said Matthew Gamette, the agency’s laboratory system director. While he said that’s already good, law enforcement hopes to routinely provide results within a matter of hours. He praised the agency’s laboratory as efficient already. But he said it’s at its limit. “We have no more space to put scientists in a desk to work. And we have no space to be able to give them analytical space to spread out the evidence and do the analysis. And we have no place to put instruments,” he said in an interview. items.body: A new training center could enhance semiconductor education and apprenticeship programs through a partnership between Micron Technology Inc. and the College of Western Idaho. Micron Monday unveiled its 60,000-square-foot Micron Training Center near its Boise campus. The goal is to build semiconductor career pathways for community college students. “This unique, collaborative training facility accelerates new-hire readiness through an intensive onboarding boot camp and hands-on training in fab operations and manufacturing systems,” Micron said in a news release . CWI has received $3 million from Micron and the U.S. Department of Commerce, covering the cost of teacher pay, equipment and classroom space. “CWI and Micron have built a training environment where students learn on the same equipment they’ll operate in a world-class fab,” CWI President Gordon Jones said in the Micron news release. “This is what a decade of partnership looks like — a shared facility, tools, and commitment to building careers that matter for Idaho.” Beginning this fall, CWI will offer advanced mechatronics engineering technology and semiconductor manufacturing technology programs at the Micron center, in addition to course offerings at the college’s Nampa campus.

items.body: Firefighters on the Claremont Fire in Boise, Idaho on July 6, 2026. Drought across the Northwest has exacerbated wildfire conditions in the region. (Photo by Brenen Helgerson/ National Interagency Fire Center) The last weeks of summer find Oregon and much of the Northwest experiencing historic drought, exacerbating what has become one of the most active wildfire seasons in the state and region, according to state and federal climatologists and hydrologists. Beyond fish and ecological impacts, drought across Oregon, Idaho and Washington is causing water supply shortages for public water and electric utilities, costing farmers tens of millions of dollars in lost crops and leaving vegetation and soils dry and susceptible to fires. Wildfire and drought maps overlaid by Oregon’s State Climatologist Larry O’Neill on Monday during an online drought and climate outlook meeting hosted by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration show the summer’s wildfires popping up over historically dry areas of the state and region. About 4% of Oregon’s total land area — 2.4 million acres of mostly rangeland — has burned in the current fire season, most of which occurred within a one-month period. Overall, about 3.5 million acres have burned across the Northwest, including fires in and around Spokane that became some of the most destructive in Washington history. “Drought didn’t cause these ignitions, but they created the conditions with exceptionally dry vegetation and fuels that favor rapid fire growth and extreme impacts once those fires started,” O’Neill said. He and Catherine Fitzpatrick, a hydrologist at NOAA’s Northwest River Forecast Center, detailed water levels and conditions in the Northwest’s rivers, reservoirs and snowpack for a 90-day period, as well as the impacts of temperature anomalies. Even with a potential deluge of precipitation this winter in what O’Neill expects to be a “very strong” or “super” El Niño weather pattern, water reservoirs in the region are so depleted that there’s unlikely to be much carryover in water supplies into next year, the two warned. “Across the Pacific Northwest we’re substantially depleting our reservoir storage, and now we’re getting into kind of the later part of August and September, and reservoirs are being emptied out,” O’Neill said. “There’s little hope for carryover into the next water year, and then as I mentioned earlier, we’re seeing record low stream flows occurring in all three states.” Anomalous heat Most of eastern Oregon and southern Idaho have experienced summer temperatures 2 to 4 degrees Fahrenheit above normal, following what was the warmest fall and winter on record for the entire region, where temperatures in Oregon and Idaho were 3 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit above normal. Most of Oregon east of the Cascades has in the last 90 days experienced “extreme drought,” a NOAA designation indicating major crop and pasture losses, and widespread water shortages or restrictions. About 4% of Oregon in and around Grant, Baker and Wheeler counties in the eastern part of the state are in what NOAA classifies as “exceptional drought,” meaning it reached historic levels, among other indicators. It’s the second time since 2000 that Grant County has received the designation. Despite being surrounded by the Blue Mountains, the area saw the lowest snowpack on record this winter. About 8% of Idaho is experiencing exceptional drought, particularly in Owyhee, Twin Falls and Cassia counties in southern Idaho. Cuts to irrigation water supply for Idaho farmers have cost them $20 million so far according to crop insurance indemnities that are being paid out, O’Neill said, but the total cost is likely to be far higher as many claims won’t be processed until after the growing season ends. In the Yakima Basin in Washington, water users are receiving about 58% of their allotment. That includes the Roza Irrigation district, which supports more than $1.5 billion in annual agricultural revenue for the state.

items.body: Reading proficiency among Idaho’s K-3 students fell half a percentage point this spring compared with last spring — the first year of the redesigned Idaho Reading Indicator exam. Idaho’s youngest students read to their computers for the second time this school year as part of the redesigned test. Idaho’s largest school district, West Ada , dominated school-level results, with five top 10 schools in the traditional districts category. Most districts with schools in this top 10 list are large like West Ada, Boise, Coeur d’Alene, and Lake Pend Oreille. Virtual schools continue to struggle, with just one school, Gem Prep: Online, beating the statewide proficiency rate. As of August 2026, the commission authorized 67 schools, including four that have yet to open. Seven were virtual. There are 85 charter schools in the state, meaning the commission authorizes 79% of Idaho charters. The rest are authorized by school districts. What does the commission do? The commission authorizes and oversees most charter schools in the state. This includes authorizing schools to open and monitoring their financial, operational and academic success. How does the commission authorize a new school? The authorization process starts when a group hoping to found a new school contacts charter commission staff. Typically, that group includes the school’s founding board, which must establish a nonprofit corporation and establish 501(c)(3) status to apply. People interested in founding a charter school can take the Idaho Department of Education’s Charter 101 course. The founding group works with commission staff to submit an application packet that includes financial planning, school model information and evidence of student demand. The group then presents to the full commission, which can vote to authorize or deny the application. The commission has only denied a handful of applications over the last two decades, at least two received approval at a later date. Before opening, schools have a series of conditions to meet and have monthly meetings with commission staff to work toward completing pre-opening steps. The school’s governing board operates the school independently under its charter, subject to commission oversight. Schools are initially authorized for six years under a traditional charter. Schools authorized under the 2024 innovative charter law are authorized for three years. The commission meets every other month, typically in Boise. How does the commission hold existing schools accountable? The commission has standards that schools must meet related to finances, test scores and graduation rates, among other things. If a school meets those requirements, they continue operating with little commission interaction for their term. Schools that fail to meet a condition typically have a year to meet the metric. If they don’t, the commission can start proceedings to revoke the schools charter. However, a revocation has happened twice. Odyssey Charter School closed in 2015 and Nampa Classical Charter School closed in 2010, both shortly after opening. Another Choice, a virtual school, had its charter non-renewed in 2022 and was subsequently forced to close. Schools in good standing with the commission can have their charter renewed for 12 years if they meet certain criteria. Renewals can also be for a six year term. Who serves on the commission? The commission is made up of seven members appointed by the Governor. Commission staff handles the day-to-day work of supporting the commission and helping with charter oversight. Who makes up the commission staff? The commission faced significant staff turnover in recent years. Rachel Burk was hired in August 2025 as executive director. She filled a series of staff vacancies. The commission currently has two program managers, a finance program manager and an administrative assistant on staff. What is the charter commission’s annual budget? (Photo illustration by Getty Images) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Aug. 24, 2026. This month, taxpayers in Texas found out how many students receiving $1 billion in private education subsidies were already homeschooled or enrolled in a private school: 70%. Taxpayers in Idaho are still waiting to get that number from a similar private school choice program that serves nearly nine and a half times fewer students, costs $950 million less and was enacted two months earlier. And it’s not for lack of trying. Between February and July, the Idaho State Tax Commission received seven public records requests related to the Parental Choice Tax Credit. A college faculty member, a hobbyist data analyst, a homeschool advocate, a former public school superintendent and two journalists filed requests seeking data that would shed light on who’s benefitting from the $50 million-a-year taxpayer-funded program. Four of those requests — including two from Idaho Education News — sought the number of tax-credit recipients who previously attended a public school. This data would test a selling point of the program: that it helps students who couldn’t otherwise afford a private education. That tally doesn’t include unofficial requests. items.body: Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images) WASHINGTON — With just over two months until the November midterms, the U.S. Supreme Court gave way Monday for President Donald Trump to have a hand in regulating mail-in ballots nationwide, a voting method he has falsely claimed is rife with corruption since he lost the 2020 presidential election. In an unsigned emergency docket opinion , the court’s conservative majority wrote the Trump administration is likely to prevail on its argument that 23 Democratic-led states do not have standing to stop his executive order to change how the U.S. Postal Service processes mail-in ballots. The majority justices also wrote that a lower court’s injunction is “causing irreparable harm,” but left open the possibility that the executive order could still be considered unconstitutional. “The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the majority wrote. The legality of a Massachusetts federal district court order, which paused the executive order to overhaul vote-by-mail systems before the Nov. 3 midterms, will now be decided by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. In a lengthy dissent, Jackson wrote the ruling “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.” The principle of courts not altering voting systems too close to the election has been eroded, she said, amounting to a “Kafkaesque nightmare.” “States administering elections and the voting public that relies on them to do so deserve clarity, not caginess or confusion,” she wrote. Final rule issued The March 31 executive order at the heart of the case in part directs USPS to direct the redesign of mail-in ballot envelopes, including adding a unique barcode. It also asks USPS to collect voters’ names and addresses from state elections officials and directs the U.S. Justice Department to investigate and prosecute state officials who violate the order. The Postal Service issued a final rule Friday detailing how the process would be carried out. Whether an overhaul of mail-in ballots for each state could be completed in time for the Nov. 3 election remains to be seen, as vote-by-mail documents are sent to voters well in advance of Election Day. A federal district judge in Massachusetts chastised the Trump administration for sowing confusion and “creating” an emergency by noticing a rule Friday that the U.S. Postal Service will eventually require federally regulated mail-in ballot voting envelopes and state data. A 95-page notice alerting that the final rule would appear in the Federal Register on Aug. 26 outlined justifications for federal requirements on states to redesign ballot envelopes and provide a list of recipient names and addresses to USPS. The final rule became effective Friday, according to the document. items.body: Update Monday with news that Crestpoint is “winding down” its relationship with Smarter By 1 Degree. Students at Eagle-based private school Freedom Academy can pursue a bachelor’s degree before they graduate high school. The path runs through Texas-based company Smarter By 1 Degree, which connects high schoolers with online college courses and participating universities. Many Idaho public high schoolers already earn some college credit and even associate degrees , but Smarter By 1 Degree says its students can earn a bachelor’s degree alongside their high school diploma by taking online courses at “partner” universities. The company touts its compatibility with a dozen private school choice programs. Becky Butlin, a Freedom Academy administrator who oversees high school students, said she was researching homeschool coursework last year when she came across the program. Smarter By 1 Degree seemed “a little sketchy” at first, Butlin said, but she later spoke with representatives from the company and parents whose children graduated from the bachelor’s degree program. “That’s where I became more comfortable and said, ‘Oh no, this is a real thing.’ It’s a good curriculum, solid curriculum, and … has that partnership with the universities.” Some of those university relationships appear tenuous, however. When Idaho Education News reached out to the institutions that offer courses through the program, one president denied having a “partnership” with the company — and threatened to sue EdNews if it described the arrangement that way. Smarter By 1 Degree subsequently removed its university partners from its website and asked EdNews not to name them. “These partnerships are important business and academic relationships, and we have intentionally chosen not to publicly identify certain university partners,” Chloe Whiteford, the CEO’s assistant, said by email . “Publishing information that was provided to you directly during a conversation … could negatively affect those partnerships.” Freedom Academy partnered with Smarter By 1 Degree last year. About 20 students are enrolled in its high school, and enrollment grows each year, administrators said. One student is scheduled to graduate in 2028 with a business administration degree from Crestpoint University. Who’s who? Freedom Academy: A private, for-profit nondenominational Christian school in Eagle. Started in 2022, it integrates lessons about faith and the Socratic method into its pedagogy. Freedom Academy began using Smarter By 1 Degree about a year ago with a small cohort of high school students. Smarter By 1 Degree: A Texas-based alternative learning company and online private school primarily serving homeschool families. Smarter By 1 Degree has students in every state and a handful of other countries. Crestpoint University: A private, online university based in Arizona. It offers coursework and degrees to students it receives from Smarter By 1 Degree, but it denies any sort of partnership with Smarter By 1 Degree. The university is formerly known as National Paralegal College. Mixing faith-based learning with higher education Ashley Meyer, the K-12 school’s founder, built Freedom Academy based on what she experienced in her spiritual life after leaving home. Unable to answer questions about her faith, she walked away from the Catholic Church she was raised in. Now a nondenominational Protestant, Meyer’s goal is to equip Freedom Academy students with the ability to endure questioning and remain faithful. The Socratic method is baked into Freedom Academy instruction to make critical thinking and learning natural for students. Teachers and administrators weave Bible lessons into the coursework. “Faith is woven into everything we do, so you can’t escape it,” Meyer said of Freedom Academy. items.body: Idaho Power serves more than 660,000 customers across Idaho and Oregon. The Boise-based utility is looking to sell its Oregon service territory, which represents 4% of its customers, to the Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative for $154 million by early 2027. (Courtesy of Idaho Power) Idaho’s largest utility is seeking a $154 million transfer of all of its Oregon service territory to a locally-owned utility based in Baker City. Idaho Power is awaiting approval from state and federal regulators to sell its Oregon service territory to the Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative, which serves 60,000 customers in John Day, Burns and La Grande across 6,700 square miles. If the sale is approved, the transfer would add 20,000 former Idaho Power customers to the utility’s grid across 4,700 square miles in Malheur, Harney, Baker and Wallowa counties. Idaho Power has served Eastern Oregon customers for more than a century, with those customers representing 4% of the company’s business. Selling its Oregon service territory would allow the company to keep rates affordable for customers as the utility experiences an unprecedented energy demand , according to the company’s application to the Idaho Public Utilities Commission. The sale will not change any of Idaho Power’s customer rates, but new Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative customers will likely see a 5.7% increase to their rates to make up for the cost of the investment, according to the utility. Without the sale, Idaho Power would have needed to raise its general rate for Oregon customers by at least 17% to compensate for the costs of new company investments and inflation. The Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative will buy nearly all of Idaho Power’s distribution lines, substations and equipment located in Oregon. While Idaho Power would no longer serve Oregon retail electric customers, it would continue to own and operate some generation and transmission resources located in Oregon such the Boardman to Hemingway transmission line, which provides power to Idaho, Oregon and across the region. The transfer is expected to close in early 2027. The $21.7 million student center will be home to CWI admissions, registration and financial aid offices. items.body: Idaho has yet another growing education gap: a CTE chasm. Yes, career-technical education is booming. But it’s growing unevenly. In bigger districts, and in areas like the Treasure Valley, students have more options, more opportunities. In small towns, CTE offerings are limited. And that affects rural students and communities alike. A new state report puts Idaho’s urban-rural CTE gap into sharp focus. Providing additional programs — and pushing these programs into small-town Idaho — won’t be easy. And it won’t be cheap, either. Peter Risse " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-943x1180.webp" class="wp-image-108603" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-496x620.webp" alt="" width="300" height="375" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-496x620.webp 496w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-943x1180.webp 943w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-160x200.webp 160w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse.webp 1152w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 300px) 100vw, 300px" /> Peter Risse During a recent legislative hearing , Division of Career Technical Education administrator Peter Risse didn’t sugarcoat the situation. “A student’s ZIP code should not limit their access to the education and training needed to support a successful career in the community of their choice.” The trouble is, that’s exactly what is happening right now. And the report from the state’s Office of Performance Evaluations proved it. The OPE, the Legislature’s research arm, looked at the scope of Idaho’s 1,103 secondary career-technical programs — to see what is offered, and where. About 40% of the state’s CTE programs are clustered in what researchers called “city” schools — a mere 15 of the 125 districts and charters that offer CTE programs. Smaller districts and charters offer a limited CTE menu, mostly in agriculture, business and marketing. “(They) are not offering a smaller version of the same CTE programs found in larger districts and urban areas,” according to the report , released Aug. 7. “They are offering a narrower set of options concentrated in the program areas that require the least specialized facilities and equipment.” Conversely — and of acute concern in a state facing acute rural healthcare shortages — CTE programs in health professions are almost nonexistent in small-town schools. Idaho’s “city” schools, those 15 districts and charters, offer 63 of Idaho’s 98 CTE programs in healthcare fields: a whopping 64% of the total. “(It) really depends on where you’re going to school and where you live,” Casey Petti, the OPE’s principal evaluator, told lawmakers. In some ways, Idaho’s CTE portfolio seems to be doing a good job of serving students and employers alike. Responding to an OPE survey, school officials said their students and local employers most needed training in ag, food and natural resources — no surprise, especially in rural communities. And most districts and charters can readily fund and staff these programs. For one thing, instructors in ag and natural resource programs command lower salaries than their CTE colleagues in engineering or health professions. In the OPE survey, 68% of district and charter officials said they would like to add career-technical programs, but can’t. And 54% of respondents said they wanted to add offerings in health professions or public safety; 21% specifically listed nursing assistant programs as an area of need. It’s important here to connect a couple of dots. Idaho is scrambling to spend $186 million in federal grants this summer and fall, phase one in a five-year rural healthcare overhaul. items.body: Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at a press conference outside the U.S. Supreme Court on April 24, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador announced Thursday his office is appealing a recent federal court ruling allowing abortions to protect the mother’s health or prevent her death from self-harm. Labrador is asking a federal appeals court to block the decision, allowing the near-total abortion ban to be enforced as written. Idaho judge ruling allows abortion if it protects mother’s health, prevents self-harm Labrador argued that U.S. District of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill’s ruling defied the U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, according to a press release from Labrador’s office. The legal battle stems from a lawsuit from Dr. Stacy Seyb , a Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist, who argued that Idaho’s abortion bans were unconstitutional because they didn’t allow abortions to protect a mother’s health, her future fertility or if her mental health put her at risk of self-harm. Labrador said Winmill’s ruling “has replaced Idaho’s law with his own abortion standard,” and that Idaho’s law does allow for pregnant patients with medical emergencies to be treated in the state. “Dobbs made clear that abortion policy belongs to the people and their elected state representatives, not the judiciary,” Labrador said in a press release . “We have appealed to the Ninth Circuit, and we will fight until this ruling is reversed and Idaho’s law is restored.” Seyb is represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice. “The Attorney General’s utter disregard for the health and welfare of pregnant Idaho residents is appalling,” Stephanie Toti, executive director of the Lawyering Project, said in an email. “We look forward to continuing to litigate this case with the goal of making it safer for people to be pregnant in Idaho.” Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license. Idaho also has a civil-enforcement ban on abortion, allowing family members to sue abortion providers for a minimum of $20,000 if an abortion occurs after six weeks or after fetal heartbeat activity is detected. Winmill’s 81-page decision said the U.S. Constitution protects access to abortion in certain high-risk cases that went beyond the exemptions outlined in Idaho’s ban. A voter-led initiative will appear on November ballots this year that, if approved, would overturn Idaho’s abortion ban and enumerate protections to women’s reproductive healthcare and privacy into law. Labrador’s appeal also argues that Winmill’s decision should not be applied to every doctor in the state, but only Seyb because he is the one who challenged the law. He said the Winmill’s decision violates the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that said federal courts cannot in most cases issue “universal injunctions,” which broadly block enforcement of laws for everyone, not just the parties to the lawsuit. items.title: With Idaho’s history, everyone should pay attention to evolving language of institutionalization
items.summary: Members of the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee and their staff tour Southwest Idaho Treatment Center, or SWITC, in Nampa on Nov. 20, 2024. items.body: Members of the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee and their staff tour Southwest Idaho Treatment Center, or SWITC, in Nampa on Nov. 20, 2024. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) People with disabilities are hearing the words ‘institutionalization’ and ‘Olmstead’ daily. This shift in the way policymakers openly discuss the segregation of people with disabilities naturally follows nationwide budget cuts to home and community-based services. If people with disabilities cannot get the services and supports they need to live independently in their homes and communities, where are they to go? As an Idaho historian and a person with a disability, it is clear to me that whether or not you or a member of your family has personally experienced disability, whether or not you have a friend or colleague who is disabled, or you work in the field of direct care for people with disabilities, everyone should be paying attention to the evolving language of institutionalization. Idaho has a long history with institutionalization and a shift back to overreliance on this practice by either federal or state policymakers presents the same constitutional and moral danger. As federal protections fade, Americans with disabilities fear a return to institutions Idaho statehood and the institutionalization of people with disabilities were entwined. The state of Idaho wasted no time getting into the business of institutionalizing people with disabilities whether those disabilities were intellectual or developmental, mental illness, verbal or non-verbal, in adults or adolescents. People with physical disabilities were not always immune from the practice. The question of whether these Idahoans were better suited for living independently in their communities with appropriate supports wouldn’t be asked for nearly a century. The Idaho Insane Asylum, the original name for what is now State Hospital South, was established in 1886, four years prior to Idaho statehood. It had an original capacity of 300 beds. In 1889 at the state constitutional convention, language was included to formally establish the hospital in Blackfoot. Idaho’s founders decided that institutionalizing people with disabilities was the only way to deal with the scourge of difference. Families were encouraged to lock away their family members with disabilities, and many did exactly that. As the state grew, so did its institutions. The Northern Idaho Sanitarium at Orofino, now State Hospital North, would follow in 1905 with a 250-bed capacity. The Idaho Sanitarium for the Feeble-minded and Epileptic came in 1911 with an original capacity of 250 beds primarily for adolescent “inmates,” a term that was used for far too long in referring to Idahoans with disabilities residing in our state hospitals. It has had an array of names including the State School and Colony for the Feeble-minded, Idaho State School and Hospital and now the Southwestern Idaho Treatment Center. As slippery slope arguments go, the day the state opened these institutions was a slippery slope toward an expensive and morally dubious enterprise. While the state’s population grew, the population of these hospitals exploded. In the 1930s to 1950s, the population to capacity issue abounded at each of the hospitals. By 1955, 1,221 Idahoans were institutionalized by the state in hospitals rife with overcrowding, abuse, neglect and doctor to patient ratios that are horrifying by today’s standards. In 1970, a report found the adolescent residents of the Idaho State School and Hospital to be living in substandard conditions. It was the independent living movement that forced the question of whether institutionalization was constitutional and if it was the best way to care for people with disabilities who had been locked away from society since the 19 th century.
